title: Chevron Stock (CVX): The Record Quarter Was Built on $104 Oil — Brent Is Now $91. What Changes? - TOP1markets
content: Dear user, to protect your funds, please stay vigilant and beware of the following scams: Stay alert and trade with peace of mind! Chevron (NYSE: CVX) trades near $201.86, a market cap of roughly $396 billion, after posting one of the strongest quarters in company history: $12.1 billion in reported earnings ($6.11 per share), adjusted EPS of $6.06 against a consensus near $5.11, and a 21% return on capital employed. Worldwide production hit 4.07 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, up 20%, with record U.S. output and record U.S. refinery throughput. But the quarter was powered by Brent averaging $104 a barrel, up from $81 in Q1. Brent has since traded around $91. Management has already guided Q3 lower, and — the most telling detail — Chevron did not raise its buyback on the windfall. It paid down more than $8 billion of debt instead. The dividend, at $1.78 per quarter ($7.12 annualized, ~3.5% yield) with 39 consecutive years of growth, is not the question. The question is what a normal quarter looks like once the geopolitical premium fades. Strip the narrative away and Chevron's 2026 is a commodity story with an operating story riding on top: A roughly $23 move in Brent produced a 4.3x swing in quarterly adjusted earnings. That is the single most important fact for anyone deciding whether to buy CVX today, and it cuts both ways: the operating leverage that made Q2 spectacular works in reverse. Brent at $91 sits meaningfully above Q1 but well below the level that generated the record print. Much of the 2026 strength has come from Strait of Hormuz disruption and Middle East conflict. In mid-August, reports emerged of a military-established Hormuz shipping corridor — a de-escalation signal. If the geopolitical premium compresses, so does the earnings base. Here is what most coverage of the beat missed. Faced with a windfall quarter, Chevron returned $6.5 billion to shareholders — $3.5 billion in dividends and $3.0 billion in buybacks — and guided Q3 repurchases to $2.5–$3.0 billion. That is flat to slightly lower, not higher. Where did the excess cash go? More than $8 billion of debt reduction, taking net debt to operating cash flow down to 0.6x. CFO Eimear Bonner has been explicit that a single strong quarter does not change the mid-cycle plan. Read that as management declining to treat $104 oil as the new baseline. When a company with a record quarter chooses deleveraging over buybacks, it is telling you what it thinks about the durability of the price deck. Management guided to specific negatives for the September quarter: Upstream turnarounds and downtime reducing production by 150,000–200,000 boe/d. Downstream downtime cutting earnings by $175–$225 million. A lower average realized price if Brent holds near $91 rather than $104. None of this is a problem with the business. It does mean the Q3 print will almost certainly look worse than Q2, and investors anchoring to $6.06 as a run-rate are setting themselves up for disappointment. Yes, comfortably, at anything resembling current prices — and this is where the math genuinely reassures. With roughly 1.96 billion shares outstanding, the $7.12 annualized dividend costs Chevron about $14 billion a year. Q2 alone generated $15.4 billion of adjusted free cash flow. Even Q1 2026 — a weak quarter at $81 Brent — did not threaten coverage. Three structural supports make this more durable than the oil price alone suggests: $3 billion of annual structural cost reductions, achieved six months ahead of schedule, with over 70% from efficiency gains rather than one-off cuts. The target is $3–4 billion by end-2026. $1.5 billion of annual Hess synergies, 50% above the original target and six months early, with free cash flow accretion exceeding the incremental dividends from the added share count. Capital efficiency: management expects to spend about 25% less capex per barrel of oil equivalent in 2026 than last year, with full-year organic capex tracking toward the low end of the $18–19 billion range. Net debt at 0.6x operating cash flow gives Chevron room to defend the dividend through a genuine downturn. Thirty-nine consecutive years of increases is not an accident of the cycle. The "Big Oil AI play" framing has driven a lot of search interest, so it deserves a straight answer. Chevron signed a 20-year, 2.67 GW power purchase agreement with Microsoft for its Kilby project serving a West Texas data center, targeting mid-teens returns, with over 1 GW of capacity signed. That is a genuine, high-quality contracted cash flow stream in a business that badly wants non-commodity earnings. But management itself called the power business early stage, with only one project at multi-gigawatt scale, and said future projects depend on securing additional customer commitments. Against $22.6 billion of quarterly operating cash flow, this is a promising option, not a re-rating catalyst. Treat it as a reason the terminal value looks better in 2035, not a reason to buy the stock in September 2026. Consensus is Buy with an average 12-month target near $217, roughly 8% above the current price, with a high of $236 and a low of $175. Recent moves have gone both ways: Morgan Stanley raised its target to $218 from $210 on August 19; Barclays cut to $208 from $216 on August 17. That divergence is the oil-price debate expressed in price targets. At $201.86, CVX sits about 6% below its 52-week high of $214.71 and roughly 38% above the 52-week low. First-half 2026 adjusted EPS totalled $7.47 — but annualizing that would embed $104 oil, which is exactly the mistake to avoid. The honest framing: CVX is priced as a well-run integrated major near the upper end of its recent range, offering a ~3.5% yield backed by fortress-grade coverage. It is not priced as a bargain, and the upside case requires oil holding up. Oil price normalization. The largest single variable, and largely outside Chevron's control. Geopolitical exposure cutting both ways. Hormuz disruption boosted prices, but Middle East conflict affected about 1% of Q2 production in the Partitioned Zone, and CPC pipeline risk in the Black Sea could complicate Kazakhstan evacuations. Political-risk assets. Venezuela and Iraq exposure adds optionality and headline risk in roughly equal measure. Refining margin volatility, including demand uncertainty in Asian markets. Is CVX stock a buy right now?Analyst consensus is Buy with an average target near $217, about 8% upside. The bull case rests on oil holding near $90+, a ~3.5% covered dividend, and Hess synergies compounding. The bear case is that Q2's $6.06 EPS reflected $104 Brent that has already faded, making the stock look cheaper than the forward earnings power justifies. What is Chevron's dividend and yield?$1.78 per share quarterly, $7.12 annualized, a yield of roughly 3.5%. The most recent ex-dividend date was August 19, 2026, with payment on September 10, 2026. Chevron has raised its dividend for 39 consecutive years. Why did Chevron beat earnings so badly in Q2 2026?Brent averaged about $104 a barrel versus $81 in Q1, combined with legacy Hess assets, record Permian and Gulf of America production, record U.S. refinery throughput at 97%+ utilization, and $3 billion of realized structural cost savings. Will Chevron increase buybacks?Management guided Q3 repurchases to $2.5–$3.0 billion within a full-year range of $10–20 billion, and declined to raise the pace despite the record quarter — directing surplus cash to more than $8 billion of debt reduction instead. What is Chevron's long-term growth target?Roughly 2–3% annual production growth through 2030 and more than 10% annual adjusted free cash flow growth at flat commodity prices, plus better than 3% ROCE improvement. title: Chevron and Halliburton Near Billion-Dollar Venezuela Oil Deals - The Globe and Mail
content: Chevron Corporation CVX and Halliburton Company HAL are reportedly nearing deals that could bring billions of dollars of investment into Venezuela’s oil industry. The potential agreements come as the Trump administration pushes U.S. energy companies to help rebuild Venezuela’s oil sector. Chevron is reportedly close to adding two heavy-oil fields to its Venezuelan portfolio, while Halliburton is in discussions to provide equipment and oilfield services to producers in the country. Executives from several oil and gas companies are expected to travel to Caracas next week to sign production agreements, with Energy Secretary Chris Wright also expected to attend. Chevron already operates three joint ventures with Venezuela’s state-owned oil company, Petróleos de Venezuela, S.A., making it the only major U.S. oil producer with an active presence in the country. The potential addition of two heavy-oil fields would further strengthen Chevron’s position in Venezuela. The move could provide the company with access to additional resources in a country that holds some of the world’s largest proven oil reserves. The opportunity also aligns with the Trump administration’s objective of increasing Venezuelan oil production and securing additional supplies of heavy crude for U.S. refineries. Halliburton is separately discussing an agreement to supply equipment and services to Venezuelan oil producers. The potential deal could give the oilfield-services giant an opportunity to expand its presence in a market requiring substantial investment to restore and develop production capacity. Many of the fields being offered are undeveloped greenfields that lack basic infrastructure. Developing these assets would require billions of dollars in investment, potentially creating opportunities for companies providing drilling, equipment and other oilfield services. Venezuela currently produces oil volumes that are considerably below its potential despite possessing some of the world's largest proven reserves. Years of underinvestment, mismanagement and sanctions have left production significantly below the country’s potential. The potential investment comes as the United States and Venezuela discuss broader arrangements involving the country’s oil resources. Long-term leases are reportedly being considered for some fields, while the Trump administration has separately pursued an interest in 17 major Venezuelan fields containing an estimated 90 billion barrels of proven reserves. While Chevron is moving closer to expanding its Venezuelan operations, ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation XOM and ConocoPhillips COP are reportedly taking a more cautious approach. Both XOM and COP continue to seek billions of dollars in restitution related to assets nationalized by the former Venezuelan leader in 2007. Their decision to hold off for now highlights the potential political and financial complexities surrounding investments in the country. The potential Chevron and Halliburton agreements follow earlier deals involving U.S. energy companies. Hunt Oil Company and SLB recently signed agreements with Venezuela, marking some of the first major deals between American oil companies and the country in nearly two decades. Hunt Oil was the first company to sign an agreement to pump Venezuelan oil. The latest developments also come amid reports of a broader U.S.-Venezuela arrangement involving majority U.S. control of more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s proven oil reserves. However, details about the structure, participating companies and how that control would be exercised remain limited. For Chevron, currently carrying a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold), expanding in Venezuela could strengthen its long-term upstream portfolio and increase exposure to the country’s vast heavy-oil resources. For Halliburton, also carrying a Zacks Rank #3 at present, increased investment in Venezuelan fields could generate demand for drilling equipment and oilfield services. You can see the complete list of today’s Zacks #1 Rank (Strong Buy) stocks here. However, developing Venezuela’s underinvested oil fields will require substantial capital and infrastructure. The reported decisions by ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips to remain on the sidelines also underscore the uncertainties surrounding the market. As negotiations progress, investors will likely focus on the final terms of the agreements, the scale of investment commitments and the pace at which Venezuelan production can recover. title: Oil Jumps On U.S.-Iran Attacks; Chevron Rises Amid Venezuela Deal - Investor's Business Daily

EARNINGS MOVERS LATE: Snowflake, Five Below, Broadcom Oil prices jumped Monday morning after Tehran claimed a supertanker in the Strait of Hormuz caught fire after hitting mines and the U.S. and Iran traded attacks for the first time in weeks. Dow Jones futures fell modestly, though oil stocks rallied, including Chevron (CVX). The oil major has the pole position in Venezuela, which reportedly made progress toward a deal with the U.S. to develop and share the wealth from the country's massive oil resources. The resumption of hostilities in the Middle East and apparent damage to a supertanker was a setback following an improvement in oil flows out of the Persian Gulf and President Donald Trump's assertion that the U.S. had taken control of the key oil route. How big a setback is unclear. The takeaway is that Iran isn't willing to live with the U.S. campaign of economic pressure amid stalled negotiations without putting up a fight. Crude oil futures jumped 3.8% to $86.60 a barrel for near-month delivery, according to CME Group data. The United States Oil Fund ETF (USO), which tracks the price of light, sweet crude oil, jumped 3.4% before the open. Brent crude futures rose 3.3% to $90.98 a barrel in Europe. Both U.S. and European oil prices have climbed nearly $20 a barrel since the war started on Feb. 28. Goldman Sachs estimates that oil traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has climbed to a range of 8 million to 10 million barrels of oil a day, about half the prewar level, according to Barron's. However, oil exporting countries have directed some of the reduced flow through other routes, leaving a shortfall of 7 million to 8 million barrels. The U.S. military reportedly targeted mine launchers on Sunday night to avoid incidents like that involving the supertanker that caught fire. After the U.S. strikes, Iran said it fired on a U.S. base in Jordan and military targets in the United Arab Emirates. Under terms of a deal first announced by Trump on Friday night and confirmed by Venezuela's acting president, Delcy Rodriguez, the U.S. will control a 55% stake of a new company to which the Latin American nation has given the rights to tap new oil fields for 100 years. A January U.S. raid ousted the former president, Nicolas Maduro, who was brought to New York to face drug trafficking charges. Since then, Venezuela's oil output has remained around 1.1 million barrels a day, a fraction of the 13.8 million daily U.S. output. However, Venezuela has an estimated 300 billion barrels of proven oil reserves, about six times that of the U.S., according to the Energy Information Administration. The Wall Street Journal reported on Friday that Chevron was nearing a deal to expand its portfolio in Venezuela, potentially adding two heavy-oil fields. Chevron, currently the only big U.S. oil company active in Venezuela, has three existing joint ventures with state-owned Petroleos de Venezuela, or PdVSA. Oil field equipment and services giant Halliburton (HAL) also has been in talks with Venezuelan operators, the WSJ said. The WSJ noted that ExxonMobil (XOM) and ConocoPhillips (COC) planned to remain on the sidelines for now. That may reflect political and legal uncertainty regarding the deal agreed to by the interim president. Reuters reported that Trump will host oil industry executives on Tuesday. Dow Jones oil major Chevron rose 2.2% to 206.20 early Monday. CVX stock is closing in on a 208.98 buy point from cup-with-handle base, according to MarketSurge. However, Chevron's inside track in Venezuela didn't give it much of a relative boost on Monday. Exxon rose 2.2% and Concoco 2.3%. Halliburton rose 2.4%. APA (APA) and Marathon Petroleum (MPC) also were among early S&P 500 leaders, rising 2.7% and 1.1%, respectively. title: Chevron (CVX) Price Targets Climb on Major Venezuela Oil Agreement - Blockonomi
content: Shares of Chevron are hovering near the company’s record valuation of $210, currently changing hands around $201. Market participants are focused on a transformative Venezuelan energy partnership that could significantly impact the corporation’s trajectory. The White House revealed a multi-decade pact enabling American energy corporations to exploit Venezuelan petroleum reserves. The initiative targets an increase in Venezuela’s daily crude production to 1.5 million barrels. US-based energy firms are anticipated to commit upwards of $100 billion to Venezuelan operations. Tax revenues flowing to the Venezuelan treasury from this arrangement are projected to exceed $209 billion. Chevron remains the sole major American energy player with existing Venezuelan operations. The company maintains three collaborative ventures with PdVSA, Venezuela’s national oil enterprise, positioning it advantageously for expansion opportunities. Reports from the New York Times suggest Chevron may unveil plans this week to extend operations into two supplementary heavy-crude fields. Halliburton could also see increased business from expanded oilfield services demand in the region. The agreement faces notable hurdles. Venezuelan political figures from multiple parties have voiced opposition to the framework. Bringing the additional fields into production will demand billions in capital expenditure. There’s uncertainty around whether crude prices will remain favorable when enhanced production capacity materializes. Oil prices remain at elevated levels currently. Brent crude stands at $88 per barrel while West Texas Intermediate trades at $83, providing favorable conditions for Chevron’s current profitability. The company’s latest quarterly results revealed total profits reaching $12 billion for Q2, a substantial increase from $2.4 billion during the comparable year-ago period. Cumulative year-to-date earnings climbed to $14.2 billion versus $5.9 billion previously. Total revenue has surged to $67 billion on a year-to-date basis. These impressive financial metrics have prompted Wall Street analysts to revise their projections upward. Morgan Stanley analyst Devin McDermott adjusted his price objective from $210 to $218. TD Cowen’s Jason Gabelman increased his forecast from $200 to $205, while Bernstein’s Bob Brackett established a fresh target of $209. Additional bullish coverage comes from Bank of America, Jefferies, and Royal Bank of Canada. The primary downside risk for Chevron continues to be commodity price volatility. Should diplomatic relations between Washington and Tehran improve, crude values could face downward pressure, negatively affecting revenue generation. Currently, the Venezuelan partnership maintains Chevron’s position as among the most closely monitored energy sector equities as 2026 enters its final stretch.
